evidence.claim: The president serves a five-year term with only one reelection, is supreme commander of the armed forces, may declare war/make peace and conclude treaties with DPR approval, appoints and dismisses ministers, and can be removed only through the constitutional impeachment process.
evidence.title: The 1945 Constitution of the Republic of Indonesia, Indonesia
evidence.excerpt: The president serves a five-year term with only one reelection, is supreme commander of the armed forces, may declare war/make peace and conclude treaties with DPR approval, appoints and dismisses ministers, and can be removed only through the constitutional impeachment process.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official constitutional text on an authoritative legal database; stable and directly governing 2022 office powers.
evidence.period_fit: Standing constitutional framework in force throughout 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Office-level authority and constraints for Jokowi as president; not a performance claim.
contrary_evidence: No nuclear-specific authority appears in the text; it defines general executive powers, not nuclear command.
Several core powers are constrained by DPR and judicial procedures.

evidence.claim: The World Bank approved a $750 million loan to help Indonesia increase tax revenue, improve tax system equity, and strengthen institutions for more efficient planning and spending; the release says Indonesia’s tax revenues and spending on public investment, health, and social protection lag peers.
evidence.title: New Support Will Help Strengthen Indonesia’s Tax System, Improve Development Spending
evidence.excerpt: The World Bank approved a $750 million loan to help Indonesia increase tax revenue, improve tax system equity, and strengthen institutions for more efficient planning and spending; the release says Indonesia’s tax revenues and spending on public investment, health, and social protection lag peers.
evidence.source_locator: opening paragraphs and first policy block after the dateline
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official World Bank release with direct policy description and named ministerial attribution.
evidence.period_fit: Directly concerns Indonesia’s 2022 fiscal-reform agenda and implementation window.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to Jokowi’s government through Minister of Finance Sri Mulyani Indrawati, who is quoted describing the reform agenda.
contrary_evidence: This is a government-program description, not proof that Jokowi personally designed every reform detail.
The release describes intended reforms and financing, not full realized outcomes in 2022.

evidence.claim: At the 2022 National Coordination Meeting on Investment, Jokowi ordered all levels of government not to complicate investment and to speed up the OSS licensing system, saying investment is a key growth driver.
evidence.title: President Jokowi: Do Not Complicate Investment
evidence.excerpt: At the 2022 National Coordination Meeting on Investment, Jokowi ordered all levels of government not to complicate investment and to speed up the OSS licensing system, saying investment is a key growth driver.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct presidential speech transcript published by the Cabinet Secretariat.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Jokowi as the speaking president and policy director.
contrary_evidence: Rhetoric does not prove implementation.
Later reporting still found legal and administrative conflict around investment and labor rules.

evidence.claim: Jokowi announced the reallocation of fuel subsidy funds because more than 70% of the subsidy benefited people who could afford it; the subsidy and compensation budget rose from Rp152.5 trillion to Rp502.4 trillion, with targeted BLT and wage support added.
evidence.title: Pemerintah Alihkan Subsidi BBM Agar Lebih Tepat Sasaran
evidence.excerpt: Jokowi announced the reallocation of fuel subsidy funds because more than 70% of the subsidy benefited people who could afford it; the subsidy and compensation budget rose from Rp152.5 trillion to Rp502.4 trillion, with targeted BLT and wage support added.
evidence.source_locator: body paragraphs after the dateline and the quoted presidential remarks
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct presidential announcement with concrete fiscal figures and policy rationale.
evidence.period_fit: Squarely in September 2022 during the fuel-price shock response.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Jokowi and his cabinet as the policy makers announcing the transfer.
contrary_evidence: Higher fuel prices imposed real costs on households.
The policy was also a response to budget pressure, not pure distributive generosity.

evidence.claim: The finance ministry said the fuel-subsidy transfer package totaled Rp24.17 trillion and included BLT BBM, wage subsidies, and local-government transport support to shield poor and vulnerable households from price shocks.
evidence.title: Untuk Melindungi Masyarakat Miskin dan Rentan Miskin, Pemerintah Alokasikan Dana BLT BBM Rp24,17 Triliun
evidence.excerpt: The finance ministry said the fuel-subsidy transfer package totaled Rp24.17 trillion and included BLT BBM, wage subsidies, and local-government transport support to shield poor and vulnerable households from price shocks.
evidence.source_locator: opening paragraphs and quoted ministerial remarks
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official finance-ministry release with detailed budget and beneficiary figures.
evidence.period_fit: Directly describes 2022 crisis response after the fuel-price adjustment.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to Jokowi’s government via the finance ministry and presidential policy response.
contrary_evidence: Effectiveness is asserted by the ministry, not independently measured here.
The package was reactive to a price increase the government itself imposed.

evidence.claim: Bank Indonesia said CPI inflation ended 2022 at 5.51 percent after subsidized fuel prices were adjusted in September 2022, and that close Government-BI coordination produced a front-loaded, pre-emptive response with core inflation at 3.36 percent.
evidence.title: Monetary Policy Review - December 2022
evidence.excerpt: Bank Indonesia said CPI inflation ended 2022 at 5.51 percent after subsidized fuel prices were adjusted in September 2022, and that close Government-BI coordination produced a front-loaded, pre-emptive response with core inflation at 3.36 percent.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Central-bank report with direct inflation and policy-response data.
evidence.period_fit: End-of-2022 macro and policy assessment for the target year.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Only partially attributable to Jokowi because BI is independent, but the report explicitly credits government-BI coordination after the fuel-price move.
contrary_evidence: Inflation still exceeded the target band.
The central bank, not the president alone, drove monetary stabilization.

evidence.claim: BPS said Indonesia’s economy grew 5.31 percent in 2022, GDP per capita reached Rp71.0 million or US$4,783.9, and exports were the strongest growth component.
evidence.title: Indonesia GDP Growth Rate 5.31 Percent (2022)
evidence.excerpt: BPS said Indonesia’s economy grew 5.31 percent in 2022, GDP per capita reached Rp71.0 million or US$4,783.9, and exports were the strongest growth component.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official national statistics release with year-end macro figures.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partly attributable to Jokowi’s government, but also shaped by reopening and commodity prices.
contrary_evidence: The result reflects strong external commodity conditions and post-COVID reopening as well as domestic policy.
Growth alone does not prove broad-based prosperity.

evidence.claim: BPS reported that August 2022 unemployment was 5.86 percent, the number of employed people increased by 4.25 million from August 2021, and the formal sector share rose to 40.69 percent.
evidence.title: August 2022: The unemployment rate was 5.86 percent and The average labour wage was 3.07 milion rupiahs per month
evidence.excerpt: BPS reported that August 2022 unemployment was 5.86 percent, the number of employed people increased by 4.25 million from August 2021, and the formal sector share rose to 40.69 percent.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official labor-market release with year-over-year figures.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Macro outcome partly attributable to Jokowi’s government, but not exclusively; labor markets also reflected post-pandemic recovery.
contrary_evidence: The release does not isolate policy causation.
Underemployment and wage levels still leave room for concern about job quality.

evidence.claim: BPS reported poverty at 9.57 percent in September 2022, up 0.03 percentage points from March 2022 but down from September 2021, with rural poverty at 12.36 percent and urban poverty at 7.53 percent.
evidence.title: In September 2022, the poor population percentage was up to 9.57 percent.
evidence.excerpt: BPS reported poverty at 9.57 percent in September 2022, up 0.03 percentage points from March 2022 but down from September 2021, with rural poverty at 12.36 percent and urban poverty at 7.53 percent.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official national-statistics release with household-poverty and regional breakdowns.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partly attributable to Jokowi’s policy mix, but the report also reflects inherited poverty structure and macro shocks.
contrary_evidence: Poverty improved versus September 2021, so the year does not show simple deterioration.
The data do not by themselves prove government causation.

evidence.claim: BPS reported a September 2022 Gini ratio of 0.381, unchanged from September 2021 and down from March 2022; the bottom 40 percent accounted for 18.24 percent of expenditure.
evidence.title: Gini Ratio in September 2022 was 0.381
evidence.excerpt: BPS reported a September 2022 Gini ratio of 0.381, unchanged from September 2021 and down from March 2022; the bottom 40 percent accounted for 18.24 percent of expenditure.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official inequality release with national and regional breakdowns.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Only partly attributable to Jokowi; inequality outcomes also reflect long-run structure and external conditions.
contrary_evidence: The level still indicates meaningful inequality.
Stable inequality is not the same as broad-based gain.

evidence.claim: The World Bank said Indonesia needed deeper financial markets, noted the 2022 budget reduced extraordinary COVID support and refocused on health and the war in Ukraine, and recommended tax reforms, a better business environment, greener downstream industries, and financial deepening to sustain growth.
evidence.title: Indonesia Economic Prospects (IEP), June 2022: Financial Deepening for Stronger Growth and Sustainable Recovery
evidence.excerpt: The World Bank said Indonesia needed deeper financial markets, noted the 2022 budget reduced extraordinary COVID support and refocused on health and the war in Ukraine, and recommended tax reforms, a better business environment, greener downstream industries, and financial deepening to sustain growth.
evidence.source_locator: key findings section with ten numbered findings
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official World Bank country report with explicit policy recommendations and macro context.
evidence.period_fit: Mid-2022 assessment of the same year’s policy stance and outlook.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Government-level attribution under Jokowi, with specific spending and reform choices in his administration.
contrary_evidence: Much of the text is analytical and prescriptive rather than a record of implementation.
Some macro improvement was due to commodity and reopening effects.

evidence.claim: The World Bank approved a $350 million loan to improve human capital through income protection, expanded health access, healthier behavior, and more effective government spending; it said Indonesia’s Human Capital Index improved from 0.50 to 0.54 between 2010 and 2020 but remained below peers.
evidence.title: New Financing Will Support Indonesia to Improve and Protect Human Capital
evidence.excerpt: The World Bank approved a $350 million loan to improve human capital through income protection, expanded health access, healthier behavior, and more effective government spending; it said Indonesia’s Human Capital Index improved from 0.50 to 0.54 between 2010 and 2020 but remained below peers.
evidence.source_locator: opening paragraphs and key bullet points
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official World Bank financing announcement with explicit human-capital metrics.
evidence.period_fit: Directly relevant to 2022 productivity and welfare policy.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Government-level attribution under Jokowi’s administration; the loan reflects state policy rather than a private-sector outcome.
contrary_evidence: The improvement in HCI predates 2022.
The report says Indonesia still lagged peer countries.

evidence.claim: Transparency International’s 2022 CPI gave Indonesia a score of 34/100 and rank 110/180, down 4 points from 2021, and said anti-corruption efforts had stagnated.
evidence.title: 2022 Corruption Perceptions Index - Explore Indonesia
evidence.excerpt: Transparency International’s 2022 CPI gave Indonesia a score of 34/100 and rank 110/180, down 4 points from 2021, and said anti-corruption efforts had stagnated.
evidence.source_locator: country score panel and Asia-Pacific commentary
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary CPI publication from the source organization that owns the index.
evidence.period_fit: Measures the 2022 corruption environment and policy trajectory.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partly attributable to Jokowi’s administration, but CPI is a perception index and not a case-level finding.
contrary_evidence: Perception scores are not direct proof of specific ruler orders.
The CPI blends expert and business perceptions across institutions, not just presidential conduct.

evidence.claim: Reuters reported that Jokowi signed an emergency regulation to replace a court-flawed jobs law, arguing global economic uncertainty justified the move; critics said it bypassed proper parliamentary debate, while the government said the law was needed for legal certainty and investment.
evidence.title: Indonesia issues emergency regulation to replace jobs law
evidence.excerpt: Reuters reported that Jokowi signed an emergency regulation to replace a court-flawed jobs law, arguing global economic uncertainty justified the move; critics said it bypassed proper parliamentary debate, while the government said the law was needed for legal certainty and investment.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting with named officials and direct quotes, republished on a commercial site.
evidence.period_fit: Late-2022 ruler action directly affecting investment rules and labor regulation.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Jokowi as signatory and public defender of the decree.
contrary_evidence: Government said global uncertainty and the court deadline required a legal fix.
Supporters said it reduced investment uncertainty; opponents said it undermined consultation and labor and environmental protections.

evidence.claim: After nationwide protests over the September 2022 petrol price hike, the president’s office said Indonesia would review minimum wage and other labor rules; Reuters also reported that Jokowi had raised subsidised fuel prices by 30% to rein in the subsidy budget.
evidence.title: Indonesia to review minimum wage rules after protests over fuel price hike
evidence.excerpt: After nationwide protests over the September 2022 petrol price hike, the president’s office said Indonesia would review minimum wage and other labor rules; Reuters also reported that Jokowi had raised subsidised fuel prices by 30% to rein in the subsidy budget.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting with direct references to the presidential office and the fuel-price decision.
evidence.period_fit: Direct September 2022 policy response to an economic shock.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Jokowi’s fuel-price decision and the presidential office’s subsequent review order.
contrary_evidence: The policy was framed as fiscal necessity rather than distributive generosity.
The article shows both popular backlash and administrative response, not clean welfare success.

evidence.claim: The Jakarta Post reported that analysts saw Jokowi’s June 2022 reshuffle as more political than technocratic, aimed at keeping coalition partners happy and filling the cabinet with loyalists; Jokowi said the new trade minister would oversee domestic goods supply and the agrarian minister land acquisition for the new capital.
evidence.title: Jokowi orders seventh Cabinet reshuffle
evidence.excerpt: The Jakarta Post reported that analysts saw Jokowi’s June 2022 reshuffle as more political than technocratic, aimed at keeping coalition partners happy and filling the cabinet with loyalists; Jokowi said the new trade minister would oversee domestic goods supply and the agrarian minister land acquisition for the new capital.
evidence.source_locator: middle and later paragraphs on cabinet motives and appointments
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Local-paper analysis with named analysts, direct quotes, and contemporaneous appointment details.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Jokowi’s cabinet choices.
contrary_evidence: The presidency presented the reshuffle as a normal appointment decree and a way to refresh the cabinet.
The article reflects analyst interpretation, not a formal finding of improper motive.

evidence.claim: Tax income had reached 110.06 percent of target by 14 December 2022 and grew 41.93 percent year over year; Sri Mulyani said this reflected good economic recovery, rising commodities, and reform of the tax law.
evidence.title: Tax Revenue Reaches 110.06 Percent
evidence.excerpt: Tax income had reached 110.06 percent of target by 14 December 2022 and grew 41.93 percent year over year; Sri Mulyani said this reflected good economic recovery, rising commodities, and reform of the tax law.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official presidential-secretariat republication of finance-ministry data and quoted explanation.
evidence.period_fit: End-of-2022 fiscal-performance evidence for the target year.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to Jokowi’s administration through the finance ministry and tax policy apparatus.
contrary_evidence: Commodity prices materially boosted receipts, so this is not purely a structural-policy effect.
The article reports achievement against target, not distributional quality.
